doc.title: Luis Conte interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 24, 2025

chapter: Leaving Cuba and arriving in Los Angeles
title: Leaving Cuba in 1967 after Castro's military decree
summary: Hearing Castro's speech in his father's car, Conte was sent out alone at 14; the cover story was a wish to become a priest, and his parents did not see him for seven years.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: I understand from your website that your parents arranged for you to leave in 1967?
Can you tell me what the conversation around the dinner table was like leading up to that?

Well it didn’t start at the dinner table, it started while I was in a car with my dad. And my dad would make house – he was a doctor so he was making house visits. And sometimes I would go with him, for whatever reason. And Castro was over there when Mr. Castro or whoever is in power now speaks everybody listens. Nothing else happens. The radio, everything is on the speaker. It’s like big brother you know. The speakers are in the street. And he was doing a speech, and he says, “From now on the men from the age of 15 are in the military and nobody leaves the island. That’s what happened. And I’m sitting here in my dad’s car and immediately I’m going – you know I didn’t know anything about – I knew I wasn’t free. I knew – it was the music was telling me you know, really you know, because I couldn’t access this music I wanted to hear from the outside for example. And anyway so I told my dad, “Hey dad, did you hear that? I just turned 14, man. I’m never going to get out of here.” And he said, “Well we’re going to have to get you out of here. I’ve got to speak with your mom and she what she says.” “But,” he says, “don’t worry, we may not be able to go with you, you might have to go on your own, but we’ll be out of here in maybe like six months or so.” Which he knew wasn’t true and I thought it was true but I didn’t see my mom and dad until seven years later, until I was 22, or even spoke with them. Because there was no communications. It’s not like now you’ve got WhatsApp and I know some Cuban friends of mine talk to their parents who are at home or their grandparents left back there. I couldn’t communicate with these guys except for telegram or letters. Anyway so that’s what happened. So my dad, it’s a bit of an old story but I didn’t have a passport. Why would I get a passport if they don’t want you to leave? But my dad knew people in the government because he had helped a lot of people during the revolution. When the revolution happened Castro lied to everyone. We all know that. We thought he was the Messiah and he turned out to be a dictator once he took over. But during that revolution you know like my uncle and my dad, they were supportive of the revolution and my dad helped some guys, being a doctor, in the City of Santiago and these guys now were in the government and he was able to – I don't know how he was able to get me a passport but he got me a passport. And he got me an exit. It’s a blessing man. I mean I’m Christian and I believe in Jesus and God man, and I think they had their hand on me and got me out of there. Because anyway I was able to get a visa, an exit – and it’s funny because the excuse that I went – you have to have an excuse. Why is this young man leaving? Well he’s going to get an education. And the government’s going, “We have the greatest education in Latin America so they say, so where is he going to go study?” “Because he wants to study, it’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
not taught in the island” “Well what is that?” “He wants to be a Catholic priest. He wants to be in the clergy.” Yeah. “Oh okay, well granted.”
Did they expect you to come back?

Yeah, oh yeah yeah. The thing is yeah, he’s coming back. He’s going and he’s coming back to help our people you know, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah – we love the revolution blah, blah, blah. That whole bit man.
Yeah. So I was able to get out.
